questions.stem: According to the Taittirīya Upaniṣad cited in Chapter 15, what are the four blessings sought through the Avāhanti homa in their correct sequence?
stem_variants: In the Avāhanti homa of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, what is the exact order of the four goals mentioned?
questions.answer: Dhana-prāpti, Citta-śuddhi, Jñāna-prāpti, Śiṣya-prāpti
questions.explanation: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad lists the four outcomes of the Avāhanti homa in the specific order: dhana-prāpti (wealth), citta-śuddhi (purity of mind), jñāna-prāpti (knowledge), and śiṣya-prāpti (students to transmit knowledge and preserve paramparā).
questions.source_quote: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad prescribes the Avāhanti homa for four things in this order: dhana-prāpti (obtaining wealth), citta-śuddhi (purity of mind), jñāna-prāpti (knowledge) and śiṣya-prāpti (students with whom to share it).

questions.stem: In the Upaniṣadic phrase 'tato me śriyam āvaha', what does the qualifier 'tato' ('after that') signify regarding the pursuit of wealth?
stem_variants: Why does the Upaniṣad pray for Lakṣmī with the word 'tato' ('after that')?
options: Wealth should only be sought after acquiring intelligence and worldly literacy
Wealth should only be sought after renouncing all family responsibilities
Lakṣmī should be invoked after reaching old age and retiring from active work
Prosperity should only follow complete mastery over scriptural rituals
distractor_pool: Wealth should only be sought after renouncing all family responsibilities
Lakṣmī should be invoked after reaching old age and retiring from active work
Prosperity should only follow complete mastery over scriptural rituals
questions.answer: Wealth should only be sought after acquiring intelligence and worldly literacy
accepted_answers: Wealth should only be sought after acquiring intelligence and worldly literacy
questions.explanation: 'Tato' means 'after gaining intelligence', indicating that money in the hands of an unwise or undisciplined individual causes evil, making discernment and moral guidance a prerequisite for receiving wealth.
questions.source_quote: The Upaniṣad says 'tato me śriyam āvaha', 'after that bring Lakṣmī to me'; 'after' here means after gaining intelligence, meaning worldly literacy before setting goals...

questions.stem: How does Chapter 15 pragmatically redefine the sequence of human pursuits (Kāma, Artha, Dharma, Mokṣa) for an individual in everyday life?
stem_variants: What is the practical functional progression of the four goals articulated in the chapter?
options: Cultivating healthy desires for body and mind (Kāma), which enables earning success (Artha), applied toward righteous deeds (Dharma), culminating in inner independence (Mokṣa)
Abandoning Kāma completely, performing pure Dharma, gathering Artha for sacrifices, and attaining Mokṣa through asceticism
Maximizing Artha through any available avenue, fulfilling all Kāma, paying reparations through Dharma, and seeking Mokṣa in post-retirement
Securing Mokṣa first through philosophical detachment, followed by Dharma, Artha, and controlled Kāma
distractor_pool: Abandoning Kāma completely, performing pure Dharma, gathering Artha for sacrifices, and attaining Mokṣa through asceticism
Maximizing Artha through any available avenue, fulfilling all Kāma, paying reparations through Dharma, and seeking Mokṣa in post-retirement
Securing Mokṣa first through philosophical detachment, followed by Dharma, Artha, and controlled Kāma
questions.answer: Cultivating healthy desires for body and mind (Kāma), which enables earning success (Artha), applied toward righteous deeds (Dharma), culminating in inner independence (Mokṣa)
accepted_answers: Cultivating healthy desires for body and mind (Kāma), which enables earning success (Artha), applied toward righteous deeds (Dharma), culminating in inner independence (Mokṣa)
questions.explanation: The text explains that natural human desire (kāma) must first be kept healthy (sound body and mind) so it forms an effective instrument to earn wealth and success (artha). That wealth is used for dharmic duties, naturally ripening into mokṣa, understood as inner peace and freedom.
questions.source_quote: ...as ordinary humans we have kāma (desire), which should not damage our health... With this we gain success, fame and money (artha), use it for dharmic purposes, and ultimately reach mokṣa.

questions.stem: What critical societal failure does the chapter identify when graduates treat unchecked Kāma as the primary goal of life?
stem_variants: According to Chapter 15, how does making undisciplined Kāma the primary goal warp society's perception of Dharma?
options: People justify any corrupt means to acquire wealth—even rebranding adharmic actions like bribery as 'modern dharma'—inevitably losing peace and genuine happiness
Society turns excessively ascetic, rejecting technological innovations and scientific enterprise
Academic institutions shut down because youth abandon professional ambitions in pursuit of instant enlightenment
Governments ban private enterprise to prevent competition between social classes
distractor_pool: Society turns excessively ascetic, rejecting technological innovations and scientific enterprise
Academic institutions shut down because youth abandon professional ambitions in pursuit of instant enlightenment
Governments ban private enterprise to prevent competition between social classes
questions.answer: People justify any corrupt means to acquire wealth—even rebranding adharmic actions like bribery as 'modern dharma'—inevitably losing peace and genuine happiness
accepted_answers: People justify any corrupt means to acquire wealth—even rebranding adharmic actions like bribery as 'modern dharma'—inevitably losing peace and genuine happiness
questions.explanation: When kāma is pursued without discernment, artha is accumulated by justifying corrupt means as acceptable pragmatism (e.g., claiming taking bribes is 'dharma these days'). Consequently, adharma destroys peace, happiness, and inner freedom.
questions.source_quote: To get kāma needs artha, and for money people justify any means, calling it 'Dharma these days' (e.g. taking bribes because everyone does). But adharma has consequences: enjoyment, happiness, peace and mokṣa go out the door.

questions.stem: In the Bhārata Sāvitrī, what core paradox and supreme injunction does Sage Vyāsa proclaim with upraised arms at the conclusion of the Mahābhārata?
stem_variants: What is the climactic realization articulated in Vyāsa's Bhārata Sāvitrī regarding the relationship between Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and the mortal body?
options: Although Dharma naturally yields both Artha and Kāma, nobody listens; one must never abandon Dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or even to preserve one's life, as Dharma and the soul alone are eternal
Because Artha and Kāma inevitably destroy human civilization, one must abandon all action and flee to the forest before old age arrives
Victory in war is the only absolute standard of righteousness, and physical longevity outweighs adherence to abstract ethical codes
Dharma and the physical body are equally eternal, whereas emotional attachments to family members are the sole cause of transmigration
distractor_pool: Because Artha and Kāma inevitably destroy human civilization, one must abandon all action and flee to the forest before old age arrives
Victory in war is the only absolute standard of righteousness, and physical longevity outweighs adherence to abstract ethical codes
Dharma and the physical body are equally eternal, whereas emotional attachments to family members are the sole cause of transmigration
questions.answer: Although Dharma naturally yields both Artha and Kāma, nobody listens; one must never abandon Dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or even to preserve one's life, as Dharma and the soul alone are eternal
accepted_answers: Although Dharma naturally yields both Artha and Kāma, nobody listens; one must never abandon Dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or even to preserve one's life, as Dharma and the soul alone are eternal
questions.explanation: In the four verses of the Bhārata Sāvitrī, Vyāsa cries out that Dharma yields both material prosperity (Artha) and desires (Kāma), yet people neglect it. He commands that Dharma must never be abandoned for pleasure, fear, greed, or mortal survival, because joys and sorrows and the body pass away, while Dharma and the soul endure eternally.
questions.source_quote: Vyāsa cries out with raised arms yet no one listens; Dharma leads to Artha and Kāma, yet it is neglected; never abandon Dharma for pleasure, fear, greed or even to save one's life; happiness and sorrow are fleeting, only Dharma and the soul are eternal...
